title: Hilbert's 16th Problem: Limit Cycles
description: The maximum number of limit cycles for polynomial vector fields remains one of the most notorious open problems in mathematics.

meta.author: Hilbert (1900)
originalContributions: Proof that linear systems have no limit cycles
meta.assumptions: 9 axioms: hilbert_number_ge_witness, linear_no_limit_cycles_axiom, H1_eq_zero_axiom, H2_ge_4_axiom, H3_ge_13_axiom, Ecalle_Ilyashenko_axiom, and 3 more. 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: Hilbert's 16th Problem, posed at the 1900 International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris, has two parts: Part A concerns the topology of real algebraic curves (Harnack's theorem, 1876, bounds the number of ovals), while Part B asks for the maximum number $H(n)$ of limit cycles of polynomial vector fields of degree $n$. Henri Poincare initiated the qualitative theory of differential equations in his 1881-1886 memoirs, introducing the concepts of limit cycles, index theory, and the classification of singular points. Ivar Bendixson extended this work in 1901, establishing the Poincare-Bendixson theorem that constrains 2D dynamics. Henri Dulac claimed in 1923 that polynomial vector fields have finitely many limit cycles, but gaps were found in his proof. The finiteness question remained open for 70 years until Jean Ecalle and Yulij Ilyashenko independently proved $H(n) < \infty$ in 1991-1992 using resurgent functions and asymptotic analysis of Dulac maps, respectively (each proof exceeding 500 pages). Shi Songling proved $H(2) \geq 4$ in 1980 by constructing a quadratic system with the '(3,1) distribution' of limit cycles. Even the exact value of $H(2)$ remains unknown after 125 years. The problem was also selected by Stephen Smale as his 13th problem for the 21st century.
overview.problemStatement: For the planar polynomial differential system $\dot{x} = P(x,y)$, $\dot{y} = Q(x,y)$ where $P, Q$ are polynomials of degree $\leq n$, what is the maximum number $H(n)$ of isolated periodic orbits (limit cycles)?
overview.text: The maximum number of limit cycles for polynomial vector fields remains one of the most notorious open problems in mathematics.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization builds from first principles in 11 parts. It defines `PolynomialVectorField n` as a structure with two `MvPolynomial (Fin 2) \mathbb{R}` components of total degree $\leq n$, defines `Trajectory` as a $C^1$ curve satisfying the ODE, and builds up to `isLimitCycle` (an isolated periodic orbit). The **Hilbert number** $H(n)$ is defined as $\sup_F |\{\text{limit cycles of } F\}|$ using `\iSup` over `PolynomialVectorField n`. The file proves $H(1) = 0$ (via axiomatized eigenvalue analysis of linear systems), axiomatizes $H(2) \geq 4$ (Shi Songling 1980), $H(3) \geq 13$, and the Ecalle-Ilyashenko finiteness theorem. The Poincare-Bendixson theorem and Hopf bifurcation are also axiomatized.
keyInsights: **$H(1) = 0$**: linear systems have no limit cycles because phase portraits are fully determined by eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix — nodes, saddles, foci, and centers all lack isolated periodic orbits (centers have continuous families of periodic orbits, but none are isolated)

**Ecalle-Ilyashenko finiteness**: $H(n) < \infty$ for all $n$, but the proof gives no effective bound — it uses resurgent functions (Ecalle) and asymptotic analysis of Dulac maps near polycycles (Ilyashenko), each requiring 500+ pages

**Poincare-Bendixson constraint**: in 2D, bounded trajectories with no equilibria in their $\omega$-limit set must approach a periodic orbit — this fails in 3D where chaos is possible, making Hilbert 16 specific to planar dynamics

**Bifurcation complexity**: limit cycles can appear/disappear via Hopf bifurcation (from equilibria), from infinity, from polycycles (saddle connections), or by collision and annihilation — tracking these global phenomena across all parameter space is the main difficulty
**The quadratic mystery**: even $H(2)$ is unknown after 125 years; the best lower bound $H(2) \geq 4$ comes from Shi Songling's explicit (3,1) distribution, but no upper bound is known
prerequisites: Ordinary differential equations: existence, uniqueness, and phase portraits
Polynomial vector fields and the Poincare-Bendixson theorem
Periodic orbits, limit cycles, and topological dynamics in the plane
Bifurcation theory: Hopf bifurcation and saddle-node connections

sections.title: Trajectories and Periodic Orbits
sections.summary: Defines `Trajectory F` as a $C^1$ curve $\gamma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ satisfying $\gamma'(t) = F(\gamma(t))$. Defines `isPeriodic` ($\exists T > 0, \gamma(t+T) = \gamma(t)$), `minimalPeriod`, `orbit` (the image $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$), and `isPeriodicOrbit`.

sections.title: Limit Cycles
sections.summary: Defines `isIsolatedPeriodicOrbit` (periodic orbit with an $\varepsilon$-neighborhood containing no other periodic orbits), `isLimitCycle` (synonym), `limitCycles F` (the set of all limit cycles), and counting predicates `hasAtMostLimitCycles` and `hasExactlyLimitCycles` using `Set.ncard`.

sections.title: The Hilbert Number H(n)
sections.summary: Defines $H(n) = \sup_F |\{\text{limit cycles of } F\}|$ as `HilbertNumber n := \iSup (F : PolynomialVectorField n), (limitCycles F.toVectorField).ncard` valued in $\mathbb{N}_{\infty}$. Proves `HilbertNumber_ge_iff`: $k \leq H(n) \iff \exists F$ with $\geq k$ limit cycles.

sections.title: The Main Conjecture
sections.summary: States `Hilbert16_MainConjecture`: $\forall n \geq 1, \exists k \in \mathbb{N}: H(n) = k$. This is the full statement of Hilbert's 16th Problem (Part B).

sections.title: H(1) = 0: The Linear Case
sections.summary: Defines `LinearVectorField` with matrix representation, converts to `PolynomialVectorField 1` via `toPolynomialVectorField`. Axiomatizes that linear systems have no limit cycles (`linear_no_limit_cycles_axiom`) based on eigenvalue phase portrait analysis (nodes, saddles, foci, centers). Proves `H1_eq_zero : HilbertNumber 1 = 0`.

sections.title: Known Lower Bounds
sections.summary: Axiomatizes `H2_ge_4` (Shi Songling 1980, '(3,1) distribution' of limit cycles in a quadratic system) and `H3_ge_13` (cubic systems with $\geq 13$ limit cycles). These are constructive results requiring computer-assisted verification.

sections.title: Ecalle-Ilyashenko Finiteness Theorem
sections.summary: Axiomatizes `Ecalle_Ilyashenko`: $\forall n, \exists k: H(n) = k$. The 1991-92 independent proofs by Ecalle (resurgent functions) and Ilyashenko (Dulac map asymptotics) fixed gaps in Dulac's 1923 claim, each exceeding 500 pages. Gives finiteness but **no effective bound**.

sections.title: Poincare-Bendixson Theory
sections.summary: Defines `omegaLimitSet` ($\bigcap_T \overline{\gamma([T,\infty))}$), `isEquilibrium`, `equilibria`. Axiomatizes the **Poincare-Bendixson theorem**: if $\omega(\gamma)$ is bounded and contains no equilibria, it is a periodic orbit. Also axiomatizes that limit cycles arise as $\omega$-limits of spiraling trajectories.

Axiomatizes Hopf bifurcation: a one-parameter family of quadratic systems transitions from 0 to 1 limit cycle at a critical parameter value. The summary theorem synthesizes all known results.

conclusion.summary: The formalization captures the full landscape of Hilbert's 16th Problem (Part B), from the definition of polynomial vector fields and limit cycles through the Hilbert number $H(n)$, the proof that $H(1) = 0$, lower bounds $H(2) \geq 4$ and $H(3) \geq 13$, the Ecalle-Ilyashenko finiteness theorem, Poincare-Bendixson theory, and Hopf bifurcation. The file uses Mathlib's `MvPolynomial`, `EuclideanSpace`, and ODE infrastructure with deeper results axiomatized.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: Hilbert's 16th Problem connects the algebraic structure of polynomial systems to the topological complexity of their phase portraits.

Resolution would require a deep understanding of the global bifurcation structure of polynomial vector fields. Progress on this problem has driven developments in resurgent analysis (Ecalle), quasi-analytic classes (Ilyashenko), and computational algebraic geometry.
openQuestions: What is the exact value of $H(2)$? The lower bound $H(2) \geq 4$ has stood since 1980; many researchers conjecture $H(2) = 4$ but no upper bound is known.
Is there a polynomial bound on $H(n)$ in terms of $n$? The Ecalle-Ilyashenko proof gives finiteness but no effective bound whatsoever.

Can the Poincare-Bendixson theorem, Ecalle-Ilyashenko theorem, or Shi Songling construction be fully formalized in Lean? Currently all are axiomatized due to their substantial infrastructure requirements.
What is the relationship between Part A (ovals of algebraic curves) and Part B (limit cycles)? Petrovskii and Landis attempted to connect them but their results had errors.

crossReferences.description: Brouwer's fixed point theorem implies existence of equilibria for continuous vector fields on compact domains, foundational to analyzing limit cycles and phase portraits.
Schauder's theorem generalizes Brouwer to infinite dimensions and directly implies the Peano existence theorem for ODE solutions, foundational to the trajectory theory used here.
Perelman's resolution via Ricci flow connects to dynamical systems through geometric evolution equations; both problems concern deep topological structure.
Hilbert's 19th Problem on PDE regularity connects to limit cycle analysis through smoothness of solutions to differential equations.
Hilbert's 21st Problem on Fuchsian systems with prescribed monodromy connects to the qualitative theory of differential equations and singular point analysis.
